caseStudies.title: Focus Vault
caseStudies.cardSummary: Designed a browser productivity extension for deep work: blocking distractions, enforcing session timers, and applying Calm Technology principles to reduce interruption without friction.
caseStudies.summary: A Chrome extension that flips the focus blocker model: instead of blocking what distracts you, it defines what you need. Full product arc from discovery interviews through PRD, metrics, roadmap, and Calm Technology principles.

content.text: When a user is trying to focus in a particular browser tab, the presence of other open tabs creates a constant source of distraction. The average user has 17 tabs open at any given time. Productivity communities consistently identify tab-switching as a primary focus killer.
Discovery method: Personal experience as a proxy user, validated through five structured user interviews. Core discipline: ask about the past, never the future.

A Chrome extension allowing users to initiate a timed focus session capped at 90 minutes. Once a session begins, the browser locks to a pre-defined group of approved tabs. If a user attempts to exit early, a 15-second countdown prompts confirmation. The goal is pause, not punishment.

caseStudies.title: Spotify: Discover Music
caseStudies.cardSummary: A fifth discovery signal for Spotify, human judgment from genre communities, surfacing music no listening-history algorithm can find.
caseStudies.summary: All four of Spotify's existing recommendation inputs, collaborative filtering, audio analysis, NLP, and contextual signals, measure past listening behavior, so none can surface music a user has never heard. Discover Music adds a fifth input: human evaluative judgment sourced from ten seeded genre communities, paired with a text-input discovery mode that can ignore listening history entirely. At 290M premium subscribers, a 1% retention improvement protects roughly $380M in annualised revenue.

content.text: 87% of streamed tracks get 1,000 plays or fewer, a long-tail discovery problem, not an edge case. Spotify's catalog has grown to 250M tracks, but every existing input, collaborative filtering, audio analysis, NLP, and contextual signals, still measures past behavior. None can surface something a user has never encountered.

Premium subscribers describe the experience as an echo chamber in Spotify's own community forums, some threatening to cancel. The ceiling isn't a tuning problem, it's structural: features built on listening history cannot discover what isn't in that history.

Discover Music introduces a fifth input category: human evaluative judgment sourced from ten seeded genre communities, Hip-Hop, Pop, Rock, Electronic, K-Pop, and more, where fans debate favorite artists and NLP extracts connections no acoustic algorithm can find.

items: Text input: users describe intent directly ('something like jazz fusion but heavier'), anchoring output to stated intent rather than a mood
Intensity filter: from 'Take it easy' (70% familiar) to 'Music from another planet,' where listening history is ignored entirely
Full track playback: serves the job of finding music to save and return to, not soundtracking a moment

content.text: At 290 million premium subscribers paying $11/month, a 1% improvement in retention protects roughly $380 million in annualised revenue. Discover Music targets the playlist-fatigue cohort, the users at highest churn risk.

caseStudies.title: Goodreads: Rediscovering Discovery
caseStudies.cardSummary: A plan to fix Goodreads' broken discovery and untrustworthy reviews using Kindle data Amazon already owns, protecting its $21.7B book business.
caseStudies.summary: Amazon bought Goodreads in 2013 and left it stagnant, 150M+ members, and a mass user exodus to rivals when trust broke in November 2024. The problem isn't a lack of resources: Amazon already owns the Kindle reading data, the purchase ecosystem, and the community. A better Goodreads is not a product investment. It is a revenue protection play for a $21.7 billion US book business.

content.text: Goodreads has two structural failures: users cannot find books that match their taste, and they cannot trust the reviews they see. A rigid five-star system with no nuance, recommendations that favor bestsellers over personal fit, unmoderated review bombing, and a Kindle integration gap between two Amazon products that barely talk to each other.

"It does feel like Amazon bought it and then abandoned it," says publishing consultant Jane Friedman (The Washington Post, 2023). Despite 150M+ members, a rival gained 25,000 signups in a single day when trust broke in November 2024.
Four interlocking components targeting both problems simultaneously. The first two fix discovery. The second two fix trust.

items: Redesigned Onboarding: a 5-question preference quiz at signup, genre-weighted highest, with a lighter flow for returning readers
Weighted Recommendation Engine: genre as the primary filter, taste signals ranking results within the filtered pool, learning continuously without new forms
Kindle Integration: already-read books excluded automatically, completion pace as engagement signal, abandoned books creating negative signals
Trustworthy Review System: multi-dimensional ratings, mandatory comments below 3 stars, timing-based spike detection, and Verified Reader badges weighted higher in public ratings

content.text: Amazon owns the data that could fix Goodreads. Kindle knows exactly which books a user finished, how fast, and which were abandoned, a feedback loop no competitor can build. At 80%+ of US ebook sales, a 1% lift in discovery-to-purchase conversion protects $217 million in annual revenue.

caseStudies.title: Notion: Guided Mode
caseStudies.cardSummary: A free, user-triggered AI guide that solves Notion's activation problem for middle users without touching the power-user experience.
caseStudies.summary: Notion has 100M users, 4M paying customers, and $600M in ARR, but the growth bottleneck isn't pricing, it's activation: the blank canvas offers infinite flexibility with no starting point. Guided Mode is a free, user-triggered AI guide that meets middle users exactly when they get stuck, without touching the power-user experience or requiring new infrastructure. Converting just 1% of Notion's 96M unpaid users would add $144M in ARR.

content.text: The blank canvas is Notion's biggest strength and its biggest churn driver. Infinite flexibility overwhelms users who haven't used database-first tools before, 80% of app users have deleted an app for this exact reason (Wyzowl, 2020). Notion offers a help centre, but no in-product guide that meets users in the moment they get stuck.

"I spent 45 minutes trying to customise a Notion template for my job search. I ended up paying for an AI recruiter instead, because the AI was easier to set up than the template." James is not a new user. He is a stuck user.

Notion Guided Mode: a reactive AI guide built into Notion, free for all users, active only when asked. It explains features in plain language, suggests templates based on the user's stated goal, and walks users through setup step by step.

items: User-triggered only: the guide activates exclusively when a user types a question, no proactive nudges, so engagement data can't quietly reshape Notion's product direction
Toggle on/off: power users can disable it permanently; middle users keep it on. Segmented data keeps power-user features evaluated on power-user behaviour only
Free tier of Notion AI: setup and navigation stay free forever; content generation and automation remain paid at $10/user/month

content.text: With 96% of users not paying, Notion's bottleneck is activation, not awareness. Converting just 1% of the 96M unpaid users adds $144M in ARR, at $0 marginal infrastructure cost.

caseStudies.title: Predictive Road-Status Detection
caseStudies.cardSummary: Inferring road closures from travel-time data instead of citizen reports, reframed as a civic-infrastructure signal.
caseStudies.summary: Regular commuters know their routes well enough that they rarely open a navigation app, so the people most likely to encounter a new diversion are exactly those least likely to be generating data about it. This spec proposes a two-source detection system, passive travel-time inference plus a municipal data partnership, that infers road diversions and closures without requiring any citizen reporting, and reframes the output as a general civic-infrastructure signal product rather than a single Maps feature.

content.text: Regular commuters know their routes well enough that they rarely open a navigation app. The people most likely to encounter a new diversion are exactly those least likely to be generating data about it, a structural blind spot that costs India's top four cities an estimated $22B a year in peak-hour traffic delay.

A USDOT-backed study matched Waze's crowdsourced incident reports against official state-agency logs. Match rates held around 40% on highways, but fell to just 4% on local roads, the exact reporting gap this spec targets.
Two sources covering each other's blind spot. No citizen reporting required at any point.

items: Passive inference: watches aggregate travel-time patterns over a few days to catch diversions that build up naturally. Blind spot: day one, before any history exists to compare against.
Municipal data partnership: a direct feed from traffic police on planned closures and construction, ahead of time. Blind spot: coverage, since it's only as good as the partnership.
Combined system: passive inference carries day-to-day coverage, the municipal feed closes the day-one gap for planned work.

content.text: Not every anomaly is a diversion; an accident or a broken-down truck produces the same traffic-pattern anomaly as a real diversion. The classification rule is the decay curve, not the anomaly alone: an incident drops back to baseline within a day, a diversion stays flat or gets worse past that window.

Strip out the navigation UI and this is a general "what changed on this road" signal, applicable to waterlogging, a fallen tree, or a burst pipe, none of which get reliably reported either, for the same structural reason diversions don't.

During Cyclone Ditwah in November 2025, Chennai saw 154cm of rainfall in 24 hours and 54 flights were cancelled across the city and three other Tamil Nadu airports. The reframe: not a Maps feature, but a real-time civic issue feed sold to municipal traffic and disaster-response departments as inferred-incident data, with navigation apps as just one distribution channel.
